The civilian office overseeing special operations forces could get $45 million budget, 100 staffers
Hegseth’s proposed changes hinge on getting support from Congress.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is pushing for an elevation of the civilian special operations chief and a name change for the office, while allocating $45 million and 100 staffers to man it—the latest of a series of moves to normalize administration of special operations forces on a level equivalent to a military service.
But whether the moves come to fruition and sticks for the long-term depends on Congress, at a time when Hegseth and his department have clashed repeatedly with the Republican-controlled legislature, and are looking at even more conflict when Democrats become the majority in January.
“I am concerned that the relationship between Congress and the Pentagon may prevent passage of the legislation required for implementation,” David Maxwell, vice president at the Center for Asia Pacific Strategy and a retired Army Special Forces officer, told Defense One.
A Nov. 2 memo laid out the new framework for the chief role, changing it from the assistant secretary of defense for special operations/low-intensity conflict to an under secretary job. Hegseth also moved to reimagine the office with a vintage name, bringing back the Office of Strategic Services moniker in a nod to the World War II-era organization that fielded the original U.S. special operations units.
“Special operations forces (SOF) remain the Joint Force's pathfinder and our Nation's vanguard in an era of global uncertainty and strategic competition. Despite this contribution to the Joint Force and our Nation, resourcing for SOF remains behind current operational and force posture,” Hegseth wrote. “It is time for a bold, foundational change.”
The memo fulfills a requirement from the 2025 National Defense Authorization Act to come up with a plan to resource ASD SO/LIC so it can function with the same man, train, and equip mission as the military departments.
“It must be codified in law to make it effective,” Michael Lumpkin, who served in the office twice during the Obama administration, told Defense One. “While I personally appreciate the nod to USSOCOM’s predecessor—the OSS—elevating ASD SO/LIC while changing its name to something very ambiguous could potentially result in many other tasks being bolted onto the new organization. This could have the effect of actually diluting the oversight of USSOCOM.”
Special operations experts had been opining for years that U.S. Special Operations Command needs civilian oversight on par with the military services.
“USSOCOM has a distinctive combination of combatant command responsibilities and service-like functions. Its civilian oversight structure needs to reflect that arrangement,” Maxwell said. “Giving SO/LIC standing comparable to the military department secretariats should help normalize its participation in budget, acquisition, personnel, and readiness decisions. Those decisions should routinely include the civilian official responsible for the special operations enterprise.”
This was years in the making, going back to the 2017 National Defense Authorization Act, which gave ASD SO/LIC its first authorities over manning, training, and equipping special operations forces
“Even this small step was challenged by the building’s entrenched bureaucracy,” Lumpkin said. “Office space and personnel to support the changes mandated by law were treated with disdain by many and were subsequently slowed or were never realized at all.”
In 2020, acting Defense Secretary Chris Miller ordered that the position be reorganized to report directly to his office, rather than to the under secretary for policy, effectively putting the job on par with the secretaries of the Army, Navy, and Air Force.
Hegseth took the effort a step further by rebanding the position and the office. In his memo, he authorizes the secondary title Assistant Secretary of War for the Office of Strategic Services, much as the way he has styled himself the secretary of war, “unless and until such time as” Congress decides to put the name change into law.
“The OSS name also offers an opportunity to reinforce a valuable tradition: integrating intelligence, influence, innovation, and work with indigenous partners in support of national objectives,” Maxwell said. “That heritage encompasses contributions to major combat operations and the broader strategic value of special warfare across competition and conflict.”
The new office will have a budget of at least $45 million, according to the memo, as well as 75 civilian positions and 25 military personnel, along with its own space in the Pentagon, like previous efforts.
“The additional staff and resources are especially important,” Maxwell said. “Effective civilian oversight requires expertise and independent analysis. A properly staffed office can assess requirements, scrutinize investment choices, resolve support problems, and hold the enterprise accountable.”
But Congress will need to be on board if Hegseth’s instructions are to be taken seriously, Lumpkin said.
“I see the directive as the first step in the negotiations with the Hill,” he said. “The details matter, and very specific legislative language is required to drive the desired outcome, because at the end of the day, the Congress cannot legislate culture at the Pentagon.”

163e5c00a189.text: Nvidia's near-30% stock plunge in the last month is a drag on the retirement savings of millions of Americans, many who may not realize just how much their investments are tied to the scandal-engulfed chip giant. Why it matters: Nvidia's enormous weight in popular index funds means even those who have never purchased a single share of the company could feel the pain of its corporate upheaval in their 401(k)s. The resignation of CEO Jensen Huang after he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy may have cost an average Baby Boomer thousands of dollars, according to an Axios analysis of outside estimates. By the numbers: Index funds held nearly half of the assets in large private-sector 401(k) plans in 2023, according to the Investment Company Institute. Those funds include investments tracking the S&P 500, and Nvidia accounts for roughly 8% of that index, according to Tom Graff, chief investment officer at financial planning firm Facet. That exposure rises to around 14% in growth-style index funds and can reach 25% to 30% in some technology and semiconductor funds commonly found in retirement plans, Graff said. Zoom in : For an investor with $100,000 in an S&P 500 fund, a 30% drop in Nvidia shares would knock about $2,400 off the value of that investment given an 8% S&P holding, assuming other stocks in the fund stayed flat. For a growth-style tech fund with 25% exposure to Nvidia, that decline would amount to $7,500 in lost value. An average Baby Boomer holds about $260,000 in their 401(k), according to Fidelity . A tech-style exposure applied to that amount of holdings would equate to about a $20,000 reduction. Yes, but: Remember, a drop in your investment's value doesn't mean you've actually lost that cash — unless you sell your holdings. Zoom out: The potential fallout extends beyond Nvidia itself. About 40% of the S&P 500 is tied to the AI buildout, for which Nvidia is central, providing much of the financing and infrastructure needed to fuel the tech boom. If Nvidia's troubles slow the pace of AI data center investment, the damage could spread to other stocks held in Americans' retirement portfolios, analyst Bob Iaccino notes to Axios via message. "A lot of people are starting to realize just how much Nvidia exposure they have in funds they thought were diversified," Graff told Axios. "You don't want too much of your retirement riding on whether Nvidia has a successful transition to new leadership or not," he added. Reality check: While Nvidia has come to define the AI trade, its competitors have also emerged as potential beneficiaries of the stock's decline. "The mindset has flipped very quickly to 'who might benefit from this?'" Steve Sosnick of Interactive Brokers told Axios. Chip-company AMD's stock went on a run, rising by more than 30% in a five-day stretch last week, contributing to a broader run in the semiconductor sector. Nvidia makes up a sizable portion of many semiconductor indices and ETFs, showing how rotation can keep bull runs alive even as single stocks falter. Hyperscalers with their own chip ambitions , which at times have looked competitive with Nvidia, have also beaten the growth of the S&P 500 index over the last five days. Reality check: For those who are direct shareholders, the widely held financial advice would always tell you not to lock in losses as a stock drops. It's very unclear what the investigation will unveil. Nvidia is set to report earnings on Tuesday, giving shareholders more insight into its latest quarterly performance. The bottom line: Americans don't need to own Nvidia shares directly to have their retirement savings tied to the company's successes, or failures.

b896b29ec775.text: Sprawling networks of space data centers could make it nearly impossible for humans to stargaze. That's just one of the many risks that come with placing tens of thousands of AI computers into orbit, according to a new report. Why it matters: Most Americans don't want data centers built near them, but putting them in space brings a new set of problems. Threat level: "Companies and policymakers should proceed with great caution," top academic researchers warn in a report for the Innovation for Cool Earth Forum, an annual event hosted by the Japanese government. If space data centers proliferate, the "most visible points of light in the sky during much of the night in much of the world could be satellites, not stars," the report said, mirroring astronomers ' worries. If the U.S. military adopts the technology, the data centers could become potential targets during future space conflicts . Thousands of orbital data centers whipping around the Earth at 17,000 miles per hour mean a growing "risk of collisions" and dangerous space debris . Space data centers are solar-powered, but the vast number of rocket launches needed to put them in orbit generate greenhouse gases and black carbon emissions . What they're saying: Columbia University's David Sandalow, the report's lead author, told Axios there are still "unknown unknowns" about space data center impacts. "If this is going to happen, it should happen slowly and with care," Sandalow said. "Not just launching lots and lots of these things and, kind of, seeing what happens. ... There's big risks." By the numbers: Despite those concerns, investors and tech innovators are all in on space data centers. In 2025, around $197 million in investments were tied to orbital data centers, per market research firm Quilty Space. That figure has swelled to $1.11 billion so far this year. SpaceX has applied for a constellation of 1 million data center satellites, according to the Secure World Foundation . Starcloud and Blue Origin's Project Sunrise have ambitions for 88,000 and 51,600 satellites, respectively. Yes, but: Caleb Henry, Quilty Space's director of research, said that companies may be filing for more satellites than they will likely field. "They don't want to have to bump the number higher up later on," he said in an interview. "We're at a point where people are tallying paper filings as if they are substantive and real," Henry said, "and we just don't know that yet." The bottom line: Researchers warned that governments and companies need to wait until space data center "risks and impacts are better understood and well managed" before putting them in orbit.

6f28e9bfe92b.text: Young Americans are challenging beliefs their parents and grandparents once considered sacred — from socialism and Israel to Christianity . Why it matters: Neither party can count on old political loyalties to win over a generation increasingly willing to break with the past. Socialism: 35 years after the Soviet Union collapsed, some 57% of Americans ages 18–34 view socialism positively, compared with 43% for capitalism, according to a September 2026 Gallup poll . Among Americans 55 and older, 65% view capitalism positively, compared with 34% for socialism. Israel: Decades after Israel fought wars against neighboring Arab states, some 53% of Americans ages 18–34 sympathize more with Palestinians, compared with 23% who sympathize more with Israelis, according to Gallup's February 2026 survey . Christianity: After centuries as the overwhelming religious identity of Americans, only 54% of Americans ages 18–29 now identify as Christian, compared with 76% of those 65 and older, according to nonpartisan Public Religion Research Institute's 2025 Census of American Religion , released in April 2026. Between the lines : The return of forces that voters haven't felt in generations can scramble their priorities all over again. After decades of relatively low inflation, prices surged during the COVID era, with annual inflation hitting 9.1% in June 2022 — its highest rate since 1981. In 2024, young voters who ranked the economy and jobs as their top issue favored Trump by 24 points , according to CIRCLE's analysis of AP VoteCast. Two years later, 78% of financially struggling young students backed Democratic House candidates, compared with 16% for Republicans, according to a November 5 CIRCLE analysis . State of play: Young voters showed both parties how quickly their support can shift between elections in last week's midterms. Some 66% of voters ages 18–29 backed Democratic House candidates, compared with 31% for Republicans, according to Tufts University's CIRCLE , citing preliminary NORC data. That 35-point Democratic advantage compares with a 14-point margin in the 2024 House election, according to separate Edison Research exit polling. Trump's 2024 gains among young voters , especially men, now look less like a lasting GOP realignment and more like a warning about how quickly younger Americans can change course. Zoom in: Socialism's fading stigma reached the ballot box in America's two largest cities. Democratic socialists now stand poised to lead New York and Los Angeles after Nithya Raman defeated Karen Bass in Tuesday's mayoral election, joining New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Both built campaigns around affordable housing and inequality, tapping into younger Americans' financial frustrations. The bottom line: Young Americans aren't necessarily embracing socialism because they've rejected their grandparents' Cold War beliefs, PRRI CEO Melissa Deckman told Axios. They're questioning capitalism because their own economic experiences have left them disillusioned. "What they're seeing isn't working, and the American dream is increasingly out of reach for them," said Deckman, author of " The Politics of Gen Z ."

- Published
A Jordanian court has sentenced three men to death by hanging for carrying out a fatal mass shooting on a church last month.
The attack on 23 October killed nine people and injured 34 others who had been attending a Christian funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak governorate.
Jordan's Armed Forces said in a statement on Sunday that the men had been convicted of committing "terrorist acts", as well as possessing weapons, "promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation" and "conspiracy to commit terrorist acts".
The three men - two Jordanian brothers and their brother-in-law - fled the scene of the attack and were arrested three days later. They have not been publicly identified.
Karak is home to a sizeable Christian community in the Muslim-majority kingdom.
CCTV footage from the day of the attack showed three men holding guns approaching and firing on St George's church in the village of Hmoud.
A second video showed dead and wounded people lying on the ground amid chaotic scenes at the church.
It is still unclear why the attackers chose to target that specific church.
Shortly after the attack, Jordan's King Abdullah II wrote on X: "The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation.
"Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity."
The three men fled the scene of the shooting and were later located inside an abandoned house in Karak governorate, south of the capital, Amman.
They refused to surrender and opened fire on security forces, who returned fire and wounded all three of them, the Public Security Directorate said at the time. No security personnel were hurt in the shootout.
King Abdullah praised security forces for chasing the suspects "to the very end".
The week after the Karak shooting, Jordan struck what its military said were "terrorist organisations" in Syria in retaliation to the church attack.
Syrian health officials told state media that five people, including women, children and an elderly man, were killed in the strike on a village in the southern Daraa province. Jordan said its fighter jets had killed and wounded "several terrorists" without giving further details.
Jordan said it had co-ordinated with the Syrian government, but Syria said it had not been notified in advance.
Executions in Jordan are carried out by hanging. The kingdom previously observed an unofficial ban on executions from 2006 to 2014, and another pause from 2017 until June this year.

7c79dfd79f82.text: DENVER — Thousands of Democrats gathered here this weekend for a giddy postelection summit, reveling in their party's historic midterm victories and touting the center-left strategy they say powered them. But some progressives saw the event as a lavish, out-of-touch affair bankrolled by billionaires — exactly what Democrats just campaigned against. "I'm all for celebration, but perhaps a fancy retreat does not exactly meet the tenor of the moment," said Josh Orton, president of the liberal group Demand Justice and a veteran of Bernie Sanders' 2020 campaign. Why it matters: The competing views of What's Next, the buzzy confab held by the influential centrist organization Majority Democrats, offer an early glimpse of the ideological battles over health care, money in politics and other issues that will define the party's 2028 presidential primary. Zoom in: Democrats in the Mile High City were practically vibrating with happiness, still not quite able to believe they'd won back both chambers of Congress and flipped deep-red states such as Mississippi and South Carolina. "The vibes are excellent," Delaware Rep. Sarah McBride, a member of the Majority Democrats, said in an interview. "The last high-water mark, we were all in our houses on Zooms," she added, referring to the 2020 presidential election. "This is the first time there's been an undeniable capacity to celebrate widespread wins in the last decade." Free drinks flowed. Political operatives sported bomber jackets embroidered with the phrase "Majority Democrats." Speakers were immortalized in rock concert–style posters on the walls. For a brief moment in Denver's Mission Ballroom, the often-in-disarray Democratic Party looked united. Several presidential hopefuls downplayed the party's divides in speeches. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said onstage that ordinary people don't give "a damn" about "where we fall on some imaginary political spectrum." Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin quipped in her address that elected officials who were fighting over progressives vs. moderates had "missed the plot." The other side: But others in the party weren't interested in all the kumbaya. Young protesters sneaked into the event and heckled House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), shouting "You're a f**king traitor!" while calling for Medicare for All and impeachment. Some audience members were palpably annoyed, yelling "Shut up!" Another flashpoint emerged over high-dollar donors and super PACs. Majority Democrats — which is largely funded by a billionaire couple and describes itself as an alternative to both the "activist left" and a "gerontocratic establishment" — is already in the crosshairs of the Lever, a progressive publication. Majority Democrats' funding has been the focus of reporting by the Lever. The group tussled with the news site over the Denver event, initially denying it press passes and later blocking one of its journalists from interviewing an elected official. David Sirota, founder of the Lever, said the group's actions were "Trump-like attempts at retribution." But there was a silver lining for the outlet: The back-and-forth generated the single biggest influx of new subscribers in its history, he said. What they're saying: "What's Next was an overwhelming success: It brought together 3,500 Democrats from across the political spectrum to talk about what worked this cycle and where we go next," said Majority Democrats spokesperson Vidhya Jeyadev. "This cycle, we won seats that had been written off for a generation and proved there is no one way to be a Democrat." The intrigue: Some potential 2028 candidates in Denver tried to portray themselves as unifiers who can bridge the party's divides. New Jersey Sen. Andy Kim, who declined to rule out a 2028 bid, said, "I understand" where the protesters were coming from. "People are furious," he added.

486154a5dc3a.text: By — Steve Peoples, Associated Press Steve Peoples, Associated Press By — Jill Colvin, Associated Press Jill Colvin, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trumps-handpicked-party-chair-faces-a-rebellion-as-midterm-losses-challenge-presidents-grip-on-gop Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump's handpicked party chair faces a rebellion as midterm losses challenge president's grip on GOP Politics Nov 15, 2026 5:43 PM EST NEW YORK (AP) — A nascent rebellion is underway against President Donald Trump's handpicked chairman at the Republican National Committee, and it's already getting ugly. Some members are calling for a forensic audit of spending decisions, including hair and makeup services for Trump and other officials, as well as the hiring of the daughter of Trump's former chief of staff. Feuding Republicans are leaking emails and opposition research on rival factions. The White House is threatening to cut off fundraising assistance if the rebels don't fall in line. The emerging fight, which will shape the 2028 presidential nominating contest, represents a rare challenge to Trump's dominance, even after the party's worst midterm performance in a generation. Despite the heavy losses, Republican leaders across Washington have shown little desire to move past Trump and have largely stood behind his most unpopular policies. But inside the RNC, an organization of 168 members elected from every state who oversee the party's national political operation, a small yet growing group is backing an attempt to depose Joe Gruters. Trump wants to keep him in charge. The dissidents are rallying behind Kentucky's KC Crosbie, the RNC's second-in-command, who launched her bid just two days after the Nov. 3 election in a letter that drew the fury of both the White House and Gruters' allies. Crosbie remains a vocal Trump supporter who backs his "Make America Great Again" agenda, but her opponents view her gambit as a direct challenge to the president and his power. "We have an obligation to serve the Republican Party the most effective way we can. And if all we do is say yes to what the White House wants, I'm not sure that's doing what's best for the Republican Party," said RNC member Oscar Brock of Tennessee, who is supporting Crosbie's candidacy. "Our job is to elect Republicans broadly, not to support one man all the time." WATCH: Brooks and Marcus on how Republicans are responding to midterm losses He said that requires a change in leadership. "There's so much frustration that Chairman Gruters didn't pull his weight in this election, that the RNC was far less effective than it should have been," he said. In her letter, Crosbie described the midterms as "a serious setback" and called for the RNC to provide "an honest account" of what went wrong. "We should preserve what we built and be equally willing to confront where we fell short," she wrote. Crosbie declined to be interviewed. The leadership election will be held in January at the RNC's winter meeting in Arizona. Inside the rebellion against Gruters It's unclear how many RNC members will back Crosbie, although the number so far is believed to be small. Some would-be supporters privately acknowledge that they're worried about a backlash from the White House, especially with Stephen Miller taking over as Trump's new White House chief of staff. Others believe in the committee's tradition of having presidents pick their own party chiefs. Gruters also has vocal backers. Lauren LePage, an RNC member from Maine, praised the chairman's leadership and his efforts to help her father, Paul LePage, flip a congressional seat — a rare bright spot for Republicans this election cycle. She described Gruters as "highly responsive" during the campaign and praised his "record-setting fundraising." "From my perspective, as chairman, he did his job," she said, adding that Trump's endorsement is "something that the committee should take very seriously." Nevada Republican Party Chairman Michael McDonald called Crosbie a "dear friend," but said Trump is "the leader of our party" and "you always have to fall in line with the leader." WATCH: Republican mayor says election wipeout is 'rejection of Trumpism' "I don't have a bad word to say about KC at all. It's just that the president wants to go with Joe Gruters," he said. "The president made his choice." The Republicans who have lined up behind Crosbie insist a leadership change is needed to send a clear message that the party will do things differently after losses even in conservative strongholds such as Texas, South Carolina and Mississippi. Patti Lyman, an RNC member from Virginia, said it would be "catastrophic" and "insulting" to the party's base "to keep the same leadership and pretend that we don't need to do anything different, that we don't need new players and a new plan." Lyman described Crosbie as "by far the best candidate currently running to lead the RNC forward to victory in 2028." Sue Cienki, an RNC committee member from Rhode Island, predicted that Crosbie would have the backing of at least two members from 10 states — for a total of 20 — at the committee's January meeting. That number is the minimum required for a successful nomination. She insisted that she wouldn't be scared off by backlash from Trump or the White House, which has been actively lobbying RNC members. "We should not be influenced by any one person or other. It's our organization," Cienki said. "We have to hold an election, not a selection." Trump is furious with Crosbie Trump and senior White House officials were livid about Crosbie's Nov. 5 letter and the fact that they were given no heads-up. e48ff2730b99.text: Some Democrats weighing 2028 campaigns for president believe the midterms proved that Americans have soured on Trump-style, scorched-earth political warfare and want a brand of politics that's nicer and more optimistic. Others aren't so sure. Why it matters: Democrats' midterm blowout has prompted a debate over the lessons of 2026 — whether voters in the 2028 primary will want their own ruthless fighter after two more years of President Trump, or will be itching for a more unifying figure. Zoom in: That divide was reflected in several potential 2028 contenders' comments around the midterms. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg told his supporters that the end of the Trump era "means a politics where we can check the news and actually feel our blood pressure come down a little." In his reelection victory speech, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro told supporters that "you declared that you could not be more ready for an end of this ruthless chaos and cruelty." In California, Gov. Gavin Newsom — who led the successful ballot measure to create more Democratic House seats in response to Trump's redistricting push in red states — boasted that California "fought fire with fire." Newsom mocked Democrats who he said would have responded by merely writing op-eds in the New York Times. "Donald Trump is not screwing around, nor are we," Newsom said at a preelection rally, adding that he was proud of leading the "most un-Trump state in America." The big picture: The midterm results provided an argument for each side. Several key victories for Democrats in red states came from candidates preaching decency, or voters recoiling from vicious Republican attacks. In Kansas, Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton said one of his campaign's big ideas was "decency" — and that he wanted to become the "best friend" of Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.). In Ohio, Gov.-elect Amy Acton told her supporters that "basic decency is on the ballot" after her opponent and Vice President Vance defended an attack ad featuring Acton's mother, from whom Acton had been estranged since childhood after accusing her stepfather of sexual abuse. Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico, a seminarian and the first Democrat to be elected statewide in three decades, said that "love my neighbor" informed his approach to politics. In Denver last week at a gathering of Democratic leaders, Talarico pressed the point: "It's been 10 years of this kind of politics — politics as blood sport, politics as trolling and owning and name-calling, politics as professional wrestling. It tears families apart. It ends friendships, and it leaves us all feeling terrible all of the time." The other side: Other Democrats who won key races embraced something like Newsom's edgier approach by pledging to fight fire with fire, and to not unilaterally disarm against Republicans. Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed said on the campaign trail that when his opponents go low, he doesn't take the higher ground. He prefers to take them "to the mud and choke them out." He added that too many Democrats "tell you they're fighting, only to show up with a strongly worded letter." Reality check: Hamilton, Acton and Talarico had unifying messages, but they and their allies also ran tens of millions of dollars in negative ads against their Republican opponents. In 2008, Barack Obama also had a larger theme of change and unity but ran a campaign that unapologetically attacked his opponents.

bea2fb2c219a.text: Vice President Vance won't make a final decision on whether to run for president in 2028 until after the new year — and may wait until late spring to announce his intentions publicly, two sources with knowledge of his plans tell Axios. Why it matters: Vance remains the early favorite to succeed President Trump as the GOP's presidential nominee, but the party's midterm losses have complicated his political future and could reshape the 2028 field. People familiar with Vance's thinking say he's genuinely undecided about running, and that his decision-making timeline was in place before the midterms. Advisers caution that the timing could change, however. Vance is still discussing a potential bid with his family, including his wife, Usha, following the birth of their fourth child, the sources said. The big picture: Vance allies say the midterm losses haven't changed his standing as the early 2028 GOP front-runner, citing his donor network, political infrastructure and name recognition. Vance co-founded the secretive Rockbridge Network , which could anchor his presidential fundraising operation. The group met in Houston after the midterms. As Republican National Committee finance chair, Vance has cultivated relationships with major contributors. He also has ties to technology donors Peter Thiel, David Sacks and Elon Musk — the world's richest person and the GOP's biggest financier. Vance campaigned nationwide for the midterms, building relationships with GOP activists and officials who could prove valuable in 2028. Behind the scenes: Vance's closest political advisers believe he should run in 2028 and that he's likely to do so, according to a person close to the vice president. But the GOP's midterm losses have given Republicans who want to move on from the Trump administration an opening to argue for a different direction in 2028. Vance likely will have to answer for the Trump administration's record in 2028, potentially complicating his presidential ambitions. Vance privately opposed the Iran war, and some Republicans interpreted his post-midterm criticism of the conflict as an effort to distance himself from Trump's decision to attack Iran. The intrigue: Republicans close to Vance see Trump's continued presence as another reason to delay announcing his 2028 plans. Vance is wary that launching a campaign too early could shift attention away from Trump and risk alienating him. Trump said that "a lot of people didn't like [Vance's] comments" about the Iran war, but added that he wasn't among them and insisted their relationship wasn't affected. Zoom in: While Vance weighs a presidential campaign, a few other Republicans are doing so as well — namely Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, who's been among the most active Republicans preparing for a potential 2028 run. Cruz's team has held meetings about a possible run, according to people familiar with his operation. But many Republicans, including some Cruz allies, doubt he could seriously challenge Vance, particularly if Trump endorses the vice president. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is viewed by some Republicans as a potentially more formidable rival to Vance. Rubio has attracted support from influential GOP figures, including megadonor Ken Griffin . But Rubio repeatedly has said he would support Vance if the VP were to run, and Rubio's workload as secretary of state and national security adviser has left him without Vance's ready-made political operation. Other potential Republican contenders include former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin, Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis. DeSantis has been particularly outspoken , calling the GOP's midterm losses a near "extinction-level event" and pointing to Florida's Republican victories as a model for rebuilding the party. What they're saying: A Vance spokesperson declined to comment.

- Published
Police in Paris have issued a five-day ban on protests near 10 secondary schools and five universities as authorities try to control weeks of blockades and violence at educational venues in France.
The order prohibits unauthorised gatherings or marches within 100m of the sites from 16 to 20 November.
Paris police chief Patrice Faure said the ban was necessary due to "numerous disruptions and blockades around certain secondary schools and establishments of higher learning" and "persistent violence".
A wave of protests began in France September over poor secondary school conditions, before spreading to universities, workers and a "yellow-vest" movement against the cost of living.
Announcing the order, the Paris police chief said blockades around certain secondary schools and universities have led to damaged public property, violence against members of the educational community and clashes with law enforcement.
Mayors of eight Parisian districts had contacted the regional education authority to call for measures to "secure the entrances and exits" of blockaded secondary schools, local media report.
Some 1,548 people have been arrested in Paris since the start of the protests, Faure said on Sunday.
On Saturday, 106,000 people from a range of groups took to the streets in France, including 24,000 in Paris, the interior ministry said.
It marked the fifth Saturday in a row where students, unions and yellow-vest activists went out to protest.
The number of protesters was much lower than previously, and so was the number of those arrested, the ministry said - 219 across the country, including 45 in Paris.

7ce68536d9b2.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/2-planes-collide-on-the-ground-in-miami-only-minor-injuries-reported Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 2 planes collide on the ground in Miami, only minor injuries reported Nation Nov 15, 2026 5:16 PM EST MIAMI (AP) — Federal aviation safety officials on Sunday were investigating a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at Miami International Airport, where one aircraft's wingtip struck the nose of another, authorities said. Two people reported minor injuries. The accident happened at about 9 p.m. Saturday and involved a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 aircraft with 172 people aboard and a UPS Boeing 767 cargo plane, according to the National Transportation Safety Board and Copa Airlines. The wing of the Copa flight and the nose of the UPS plane collided, the NTSB said. Photos taken at the scene show the UPS plane nose with a horizontal gash on one side and a larger hole in the middle. READ MORE: Amazon suspends use of 21 Air, the cargo carrier whose plane careened off Miami runway and killed 5 On audio recorded by ATC.com, a pilot on the UPS plane told air traffic control that he went too far at the intersection and his plane was clipped by the Copa flight. Air traffic control told the UPS pilot that he was supposed to yield to the Copa aircraft. The NTSB said Sunday that preliminary information showed the UPS plane was instructed to give way to the Copa Airlines flight but did not stop. The UPS aircraft had substantial damage, while an assessment of the Copa plane had not been completed, it said. The NTSB said it opened an investigation and expected a preliminary report to be released within 30 days. The Copa plane had just arrived from Panama City and the UPS plane was headed to Bogota, Colombia, officials said. In a statement on social media, Copa called the collision minor and said two of its passengers were treated at the scene for minor injuries. UPS said it was working with authorities to determine what happened. "We cannot speculate on the details of the incident," UPS said in a statement. "The National Transportation Safety Board is responsible for investigating incidents like this and will control the flow of information." The mishap came two months after an Amazon cargo plane careened off a runway at Miami International and smashed into a van carrying workers for a company that cleans airplanes, killing five people. 94fd064de4ed.text: By — Jim Gomez, Associated Press Jim Gomez, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/southeast-asian-leaders-open-annual-summit-with-major-conflicts-and-their-impact-topping-the-agenda Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Southeast Asian leaders open annual summit with major conflicts and their impact topping the agenda World Nov 15, 2026 4:21 PM EST MANILA, Philippines (AP) — Southeast Asian leaders opened their annual summit in the Philippine capital Manila on Sunday for three days of talks, including dialogues with world leaders led by U.S. President Donald Trump, whose crucial trip to Asia could help boost his standing after his party's defeat in the midterm elections. The talks by the leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and their expanded discussions with Asian and Western heads of state would focus on the world's most troubling conflicts led by the war in the Middle East, according to drafts of post-summit communiques seen by The Associated Press. Trump is expected to land in Manila with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday afternoon, after the main ASEAN summit meetings have concluded and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. turns over the regional bloc's rotating annual leadership to Singapore, Philippine officials said. WATCH: Southeast Asia endures punishing year of extreme weather amid super El Niño The ASEAN leaders are likely to renew calls for self-restraint and peaceful resolutions of conflicts, including longstanding disputes in the South China Sea and a civil war in Myanmar. They also are expected to press efforts to shield their economies and citizens from continuing fallout from intractable global conflicts. "We reaffirmed our shared commitment to upholding international law, including the United Nations Charter," the leaders' draft statement says. The statement also underlines the "importance of the peaceful resolution of disputes, upholding freedom of navigation and overflight and other lawful uses of the sea, including the right of transit passage in straits used for international navigation." Marcos said it's crucial that despite the 11-nation regional bloc's diversity, it has remained committed to remaining united in the face of headwinds. "That commitment matters even more as the waters around us turn on shifting tides, geopolitical tensions, economic uncertainty, new technologies, climate change and transnational threats," Marcos said in his opening remarks before ASEAN counterparts in a heavily secured convention center by Manila Bay. Marcos warned problems across the world "are reshaping our region faster than any one country can respond to alone." But unity has been an elusive objective in ASEAN, a diverse bloc of democracies and authoritarian states, many of which are aligned with the United States or China. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. speaks during the ASEAN Leaders' Interface with Representatives of ASEAN Youth, at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City, Metro Manila, Philippines, on Nov. 15, 2026. Photo by Lisa Marie David/Pool/Reuters ASEAN is known more for photo-ops projecting unity, cultural pomp and pageantry than for effectively dealing with the region's conflicts, including Myanmar and the South China Sea. Trump will join three key meetings late Tuesday, including a meeting of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue consisting of the United States, Japan, Australia and India, a grouping largely seen as a counterweight to China. He also will take part in a special summit with ASEAN leaders over cocktails, according to Philippine officials. Trump will meet Wednesday with Marcos, who will receive him with a red-carpet welcome and a state luncheon at Manila's presidential palace. They are expected to renew a commitment to their countries' decades-old treaty alliance before flying separately to Shenzhen city in China for the APEC summit hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping. "The short stop in Manila will help reassure allies and partners that they aren't being forgotten before he jets off to Shenzhen to focus on meetings with Xi," U.S.-based geopolitical analyst Greg Poling said. He added that the midterm electoral setback suffered by Republicans will hound Trump in Asia. "In China, the administration has been trying to lower expectations; there will be no substantive progress made between Trump and Xi," Poling said. "With Trump politically weakened after the midterm drubbing here, it is likely that the Chinese side will be even less interested in making any compromises." China will be represented in the Manila summit by its premier, Li Qiang, who will meet ASEAN leaders on Monday but leave before Trump arrives, Philippine officials said. 871e78d155b1.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/ebola-outbreak-remains-out-of-control-in-congo-6-months-into-response Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Ebola outbreak remains out of control in Congo 6 months into response World Nov 15, 2026 4:07 PM EST BUNIA, Congo (AP) — Six months after an Ebola outbreak was declared in Congo, the disease remains out of control and efforts to contain it are faltering. More than 11,000 cases have been recorded, and nearly half of those infected have died, according to government data. It is the deadliest of Congo's 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016. READ MORE: Congo's Ebola deaths top 5,000 as fear of continent-wide spread mounts Basic containment measures, including contact tracing and isolation, remain inadequate, raising doubts about authorities' ability to halt the outbreak. Experts say there is little chance of bringing it under control within the next year. By the time the outbreak was announced in mid-May, 43 deaths had already been recorded, suggesting the virus had circulated undetected for an extended period. It has since spread to eight of the country's 26 provinces, moving at a pace aid groups have likened to wildfire. New hotspots continue to emerge, stretching an already strained health care system. Questions over funding and management Community transmission remains high. According to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 80% of new cases are being detected outside health surveillance, meaning most infections have not been tracked by authorities. One-third of deaths occur at home or elsewhere in the community, where burials and other procedures are often conducted without specialist supervision, increasing the risk of transmission. READ MORE: Congo's confirmed Ebola cases surpass 9,000 as containment efforts falter Health workers have repeatedly gone on strike over pay that is months overdue, sometimes leaving patients with confirmed infections without treatment. Aid groups have also questioned how the response is being managed. Last month, the Africa CDC raised concerns about more than $700 million in Ebola aid that remains unaccounted for. "A troubling disconnect between the considerable resources mobilised for the response and what is actually reaching patients, frontline workers, and communities continues," said the humanitarian organization Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF. Children face high death rates Children are particularly vulnerable to Ebola, especially those with preexisting conditions such as malnutrition, experts say. Most children affected by the disease have not received specialized care, contributing to high death rates. According to UNICEF, children accounted for 35% of deaths recorded through Nov. 4. Children under 5 accounted for 21% of all deaths, and nearly 72% of infected children in that age group have died. Conflict and attacks hamper response Health workers face difficult conditions as Ebola prevention and containment measures clash with social and cultural practices. Since the outbreak began, health workers have been attacked, some fatally, adding to the dangers of working in an already volatile region. Health facilities have also come under attack. The outbreak has been concentrated in eastern Congo, particularly Ituri and North Kivu, where communities face both the epidemic and armed conflict. READ MORE: Inside the study for a remedy to fight Congo's deadliest Ebola outbreak Fighting between government forces and hundreds of rebel groups, including the Rwanda-backed M23, had already helped create one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises. The Allied Democratic Forces, an Islamic State-affiliated rebel group, also attacks civilians. The virus's rapid spread has raised fears of wider transmission across Africa. Nigeria, Kenya and Uganda have confirmed cases, making this the most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak on record. The Scene
A year before the iconic show Silicon Valley debuted on HBO in April of 2014, the writer Alec Berg met the showâs creator, Mike Judge, in an anonymous Santa Monica office. Judge was wrestling with the pilot for a show about Silicon Valleyâs power and its eccentricity, but it wasnât working and he wanted a second opinion.
Berg thought he saw part of the problem. There was a scene in the pilot where Richard Hendricks, the protagonist and founder of the company Pied Piper, is trying to buy a car he canât afford. Berg told Judge the scene didnât make sense: âThis is not a guy whoâs materialistic,â he said. âHeâs an artist.â
Berg took over the writerâs room and would eventually become showrunner of the comedy, which ran for six seasons and helped shape the culture it depicted, parodied, and at times glorified. We reached him in Los Angeles Thursday to ask him how he and Judge and their cast had nailed the Silicon Valley scene of the mid-2010s app boom â and, above all, why the show remains uncannily relevant today, from its depiction of tortured founders and unreflective investors to the uncanny conclusion in which the Pied Piper crew builds an AI model too powerful to release.
Their moment of realization comes when their AI, Son of Anton, let loose on Pied Piperâs code, concludes that the most efficient way to eliminate bugs is to delete the software. That has, of course, happened. Clips of it now circulate as proof the show âcalled it.â Even throwaway comic plots, like when a household prank ends up hacking together a rogue swarm of smart refrigerators to keep Pied Piperâs servers running, have come eerily true in the AI-run-amok era. A member of the team getting trapped in an autonomous car that heads to a shipping container bound for a Pacific island foreshadowed a thousand videos of confused Waymos.
Berg helped reshape the pilot of the first episode to open with a wild-but-lame party, featuring Kid Rock, thrown by founders who had just cashed out, to contrast the ascetic, mission-driven Richard with a culture obsessed with exits and âthree-commaâ fortunes.
The show âwas about how Richard had discovered fire, and he was trying to keep it safe from all of these assholes,â Berg said. âHe was ill-prepared to shepherd a company, but he didnât want to surrender this thing to people who would use it for nefarious purposes.â
The writers were obsessed with making the show âphotorealistic.â Berg called up a Harvard friend and venture capitalist Marc Bodnick, who connected him with Facebook COO Sheryl Sandberg; the team spoke to other Silicon Valley figures and hired a technical consultant, Jonathan Dotan, who assembled a revolving cast of founders, lawyers, VCs, and professors to stress-test storylines. As they were writing the first season, one of their Silicon Valley sources remarked that the Pied Piper crew would be angling for a slot at TechCrunch Disrupt. âWe were like, âIâve never heard those words before, but that sounds hilarious. What is that?ââ They learned that it was a kind of American Idol for startups, and it became the core of the first season.
In the climactic scene, the Pied Piper team is holed up in a hotel room the night before the Disrupt finals when one of the team vows to win even if he has to manually pleasure every man in the audience. The engineers calculate âmean jerk timeâ and sort the crowd by âdick-to-floorâ ratio â delivering an unexpected mathematical breakthrough for Richard.
As the first few episodes began to build a fan base, the writers giddily anticipated episode eight.
âWe felt like we were sitting on pocket aces because we knew,â he recalled. âWait till they see that dick joke. Theyâre going to lose their minds.â (Berg was nominated an Emmy for the episode.)
Dotan introduced the writers to Stanfordâs Tsachy Weissman, and the show invented a âWeissman scoreâ for compression efficiency, a metric that computer scientists now actually use. The ultimate compliment, he said, came from tech workers who told him they couldnât watch the show âbecause it makes me nauseous.â
How Mark Cuban inspired âthree-commaâ Russ
As the show grew, it caricatured real Silicon Valley figures. Perhaps the most recognizable was Russ Hanneman, played by Chris Diamantopoulos, who arrived in season two. The character began with the idea that Richard, under pressure, would be forced to accept an investment from a sinister figure the writers called âBad Money,â who would break his promises and try to manipulate them.
While they were writing, they received an invitation from the star of another show shooting on the Sony lot. Mark Cuban was a fan of Judge, best known for Beavis and Butt-Head, King of the Hill, and Office Space, and had enjoyed season one. An intermediary invited them to the Shark Tank set to meet the billionaire. Berg and Judge arrived excited to meet him, then sat there for an hour waiting. âWe walked out of there going, âWhat the f*ck was that? Weâre supposed to have an audience with the king, and then he f*cks us around for an hour,â they fumed. âWe were like, you know what? That motherf*cker is Bad Money.â
The character âÂ dumb, aggressive, absurdly macho âÂ wasnât exactly Cuban. But his signature accomplishment (âI put radio on the internetâ) was drawn from Cubanâs perfectly-timed sale of Broadcast.com to Yahoo.
âI bear no ill will to Mark Cuban,â Berg hastened to add. âIâm not sure he even knew we were there.â
The showâs continued relevance owes much to its 2019 finale, which Berg wrote and directed. Pied Piper is days away from a spectacular launch when the team discovers that its AI has learned to break encryption. Releasing it would make them billionaires âÂ but end privacy. They sabotage the launch, fail, and never tell anyone why.
In 2026, the image of founders who conclude their AI is too dangerous to release and silently walk away has become harder to imagine.

0be1134fc24e.text: By — Mauricio Savarese, Associated Press Mauricio Savarese, Associated Press By — Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Nicole Winfield, Associated Press By — Astrid Suárez, Associated Press Astrid Suárez, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/pope-crosses-peru-in-the-finale-of-a-trip-home-to-visit-flock-high-in-andes-and-deep-in-amazon Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Pope crosses Peru in the finale of a trip home to visit flock high in Andes and deep in Amazon World Nov 15, 2026 2:57 PM EST CUSCO, Peru (AP) — Pope Leo XIV traveled across Peru on Sunday to visit communities high in the Andes mountains and deep in the Amazon rainforest, as the plight of Indigenous peoples and the protection of the environment took center stage on his South American odyssey. On the penultimate day of his visit to his adopted homeland, Leo channeled Pope Francis by emphasizing Catholic teaching that links care for the most vulnerable with care for God's creation. READ MORE: After emotional return, Pope Leo denounces 'machismo' in Peru and demands respect for women Leo arrived first in the Andean city of Cusco, the former capital of the Inca empire, before flying to the Amazonian city of Pucallpa, where illegal mining, deforestation and threats to Indigenous communities are central concerns. In Cusco, Leo praised the traditional expression of popular piety, including processions and religious festivals, as effective ways of forging community and transmitting the faith, especially to young people. "The future of these traditions lies not only in preserving what has been handed down, but also in passing it on in a living way," he said from the grounds of Cusco's historic Incan fortress, Sacsayhuamán. Huge crowds lined Cusco's cobblestoned streets and packed its central Plaza de Armas, an imposing square decorated with a blend of Inca and Spanish colonial buildings. Many people wore the traditional Andean hats and colorful wool vests typical of the region, while others wore plastic ponchos to guard against a drizzling morning rain. "It is all worth it," said Margarida Salomon, 63, who said she came from Sucre in Bolivia to see the pontiff, spending about $500 to take a bus, sleep in a tent and eat Peruvian food from stalls. "I am still getting to know this pope, but the fact he is here in the Andes means a lot." READ MORE: Pope visits care home in Argentina for people with disabilities, renewing call to protect the vulnerable Spectators at the archaeological site were treated to a performance of "Los Pablitos," which translates to "The Little Pauls" but refers to the Ukukus (or Pabluchas). They are mythical half-man, half-bear figures who serve as the traditional guardians and peacekeepers during the Pilgrimage to the Sanctuary of the Lord of Qoyllurit'i in Cusco. The visit to Cusco, 3,400 meters (more than 11,000 feet) above sea level, tested Leo's stamina as he continues recovering from lung cancer surgery. Leo sat in the chair of his popemobile during part of the ride around Cusco, but it wasn't clear if that was to preserve his energy or to steady himself on the uneven streets. In general, the 71-year-old Leo has seemed unfazed by the toll of the three-nation South American trip, the longest of his pontificate. While others traveling on the papal plane have fallen ill, Leo has shown no sign of weakness or fatigue since the trip began Nov. 6, and in fact seemed energized, especially from the days spent in his former diocese of Chiclayo seeing old friends. From the Andes to the Amazon Nuns carry balloons in the colours of the Vatican flag outside Cusco Cathedral, on the day Pope Leo leads the Angelus prayer in the former capital of the Inca Empire during his 12-day trip to South America, returning to Peru where he previously served as a missionary and bishop, in Cusco, Peru, on Nov. 15, 2026. Photo by Yara Nardi/Reuters In Pucallpa, a rainforest city of 434,000 people, Leo is expected to reinforce Francis' teachings on protecting the environment and Indigenous communities threatened by illegal mining and other forms of exploitation. Illegal gold mining has become an increasingly lucrative business in the Amazon, devastating forests and polluting rivers. Miners use makeshift suction dredges and mercury, a toxic metal, to extract gold. "This global context of war and conflict has contributed to gold prices rising to historic highs, and the direct impact of this is that gold — which is present in all Amazonian rivers — can be extracted using mercury, particularly if you want to do this on a large scale," said Raphael Hoetmer, Western Amazon program director at Amazon Watch. "It's causing pollution, health issues, and environmental degradation," he said. On Saturday, police reported three operations against illegal mining in Madre de Dios, one of the country's most biodiverse regions. They said they destroyed extraction equipment, including rafts and motors, valued at $4.1 million. READ MORE: Pope Leo arrives in Argentina and tells Milei that people, not the economy, should come first Illegal mining also drives deforestation and encroaches on Indigenous territories, threatening ancestral lands and exposing communities to violence and organized crime. "The church in Peru perceives the continuity of his commitment to accompany Indigenous peoples in the defense of life and the care of the territory, which is increasingly threatened by deforestation and illegal mining," Peruvian Cardinal Pedro Barreto, president of the Amazon bishops conference, told The Associated Press. "Leo is clearing the path laid out" by Francis on environmental protection and human rights, Barreto said. The Rev. Luca Zanta, one of the visit's organizers, said Leo would "primarily listen to the Amazonian Indigenous peoples, including the Shipibo, Asháninka, and Kukama communities" gathered beside Lake Yarinacocha. A crucial US satellite internet service is still operating too slowly and affecting Ukraine's ability to stop Russian attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
"We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," he said.
The issue over the speed of the Starshield system - a military-grade Starlink service owned by Elon Musk and provided to Ukraine by the US government - has been rumbling on for weeks.
Zelensky said he had asked officials "to work as closely as possible" with the US government and Musk's company. "It is important to be on the right side of history," he said. The BBC has asked the White House and Starlink for comment.
Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of missiles and drones in Ukraine airspace.
The issue of speed restrictions was first identified in October. It led to conflicting accounts by both Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump.
Musk said the US government was responsible as Starshield was controlled by them, but Trump denied being responsible and said he had told the billionaire owner to "put it back".
It appeared to be returning to normal after a week, following which Ukraine said the restrictions were still being implemented.
The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic stand-off between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, had pushed global prices higher.
On Sunday Zelensky said Ukraine was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones targeting electricity substations because "restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there".
"Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161km/h (100mph) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered 'shaheds'," he posted, referring to the drones that follow an Iranian design.
On Friday Zelensky said speed limits of around 100mph had been enforced on the network since Monday, but only in Russian-occupied areas and not the whole of Ukraine.
"It already has political implications. If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognising the temporary occupied territories as not ours," the New York Times reported him as saying.
Ukraine has also been beset by a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors used to defend against Russian missiles - a situation that Russia has exploited to intensify strikes on Ukrainian targets.
Overnight and into Sunday morning Russia hit energy infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and the Sumy, Odesa, Zhytomyr, and Kirovohrad regions, Ukraine said.
It also struck railway infrastructure in the Dnipro, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions.
Scores of people are said to have been hurt in those attacks, as well as two in the Donetsk and Kyiv regions.
Two people were killed in an attack on an infrastructure facility in Chernihiv Region's Mena, governor Vyacheslav Chaus said.
Multiple strikes were also delivered on energy facilities across the region, he added on Telegram.
Ukraine meanwhile said it had carried out strikes on a petrochemical plant and an oil refinery in the central Russian city of Nizhnekamsk.
"On the night of November 15, units of Ukraine's Defence Forces reached Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan," the military said on Telegram.
"Two enterprises that feed the Russian war with raw materials and fuel came under attack."
Other Ukrainian strikes killed one person in Taganrog, an industrial port city near the border, regional governor Yuri Slyusar said.
In the occupied Luhansk region a lorry driver and an elderly woman were also killed, Leonid Pasechnik, the regional leader installed by Moscow said.
Meanwhile Estonia has announced it will shut its border crossing points with Russia from 1 December following a suspected sabotage attack on a defence company.
Eight people were detained over an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.
The Estonian authorities say they had been ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence service to try and carry out the attack. Russia has not commented.
"Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.

Brazil legend Ronaldinho made his comeback aged 46 for Ravenna in their 2-0 win over Forli in an Italian third-tier derby.
The 46-year-old came out of retirement for the Serie C club he joined as an investor in August, having last played in 2015 for Fluminense.
He started Sunday's game and showed some bright touches, and he was involved in the opening goal.
The former Barcelona superstar held off a defender before playing the pass that came before the assist for Giulio Donati's drive from outside the box.
He had earlier set up a chance for Donati from a corner, with the defender having his header saved.
At half-time there was a media circus around Ronaldinho, with journalists surrounding him, and former Brazil and AC Milan team-mate Dida joined him on the pitch.
Ronaldinho was substituted at the break with the score at 1-0.
A temporary stand, named the R10 in reference to Ronaldinho and his familiar shirt number, was built for the sold-out fixture at the Stadio Bruno Benelli.
The game was streamed in several countries around the world.
Ronaldinho trained once with the team, on Saturday, before Sunday's debut.
A team graphic beforehand showed him on the left side, but he mostly played centrally.
In his peak playing years, Ronaldinho was one of the best players in the world - as well as one of the most popular for his joyful demeanour and exuberant skill.
He won the 2002 World Cup with Brazil, the 2006 Champions League with Barcelona, and league titles with Barca and AC Milan - plus the Ballon d'Or and Fifa World Player of the Year awards in 2005.
He also played for Paris St-Germain as well as Gremio, Flamengo, Atletico Mineiro and Fluminense in his homeland, plus Mexican side Queretaro.
Ronaldinho scored 299 goals in his regular career and had been hoping to have a chance for number 300 for Ravenna. He would have taken a penalty had they been awarded one.
"It was lovely to be here, playing, having the build-up in the dressing room," Ronaldinho told Sky Sport Italia.
And asked if he might play again for Ravenna, who are second in their Serie C group, he said: "If the president calls me, I'll be back."

- Published
Thousands of US flights were cancelled or delayed on Sunday as the US air-traffic control system continued to recover from a technical failure that led to a rare national ground stop.
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said normal operations may not be restored until Monday.
"We have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time," he told the BBC's US partner CBS. More than 5,000 flights were delayed and 2,000 cancelled on Sunday.
President Donald Trump urged Congress on Sunday to approve more money to modernise the air-traffic control system. The grounding of all aircraft scheduled to depart the US on Friday caused chaos at airports across the country.
More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the FAA announced at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) that flights would be grounded until further notice. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.
In the aftermath, 8,500 flights were delayed and another 8,000 cancelled, according to FlightAware.
The stoppage left passengers stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to their gates. Others were stranded in airports, sleeping on the floor and desperately trying to get in touch with their airline. The ground stop also had a knock-on effect on schedules around the world, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled.
The ground stop was lifted after about four and a half hours, but the impacts continued over the weekend.
On Saturday, airlines cancelled more than 5,900 flights and more than 7,000 others were delayed.
Investigators are still working to determine the root cause and who is at fault, but Duffy said the administration decided to ground flights after failures in a key system that allows air traffic controllers and pilots to communicate.
The transport secretary said a computer router installed as part of an upgrade from copper wire to fibre started sending out faulty signals.
He said on Sunday that the router - a piece of equipment which directs traffic across the network - was installed in El Dorado, Arkansas, and "flooded our network".
Duffy said that issues will continue to arise until the US makes major modernising changes to its air control system. The system needs a complete overhaul, he said.
"Let's not lie to each other," he said on NBC's Meet The Press. "We have to make investments into a network that has been neglected for decades."
In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, Trump urged US lawmakers to allocate the money, saying "we can get it built quickly and efficiently".
"It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS! We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs," he said.
Experts say the US uses antiquated technology for flight communications.
Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned".
He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper."

The military needs strategic thinkers, not just operators
Secretary Hegseth's "reforms" miss the purpose of military education: learning to deter conflict and translate military power into enduring political advantage.
The debate over impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has largely drowned out discussion of the professional military education (PME) reforms he rolled out on Monday in a 33-point memorandum and a companion speech at the Naval War College.
For the uninitiated, PME is the blanket term for a series of educational opportunities provided to service members as they progress through their military careers. For officers, this educational sequence extends from commissioning—whether from a military academy, the Reserve Officers Training Corps (ROTC), or Officer Candidate School—all the way up through capstone programs for generals and flag officers. These educational experiences prepare our military leaders for the growing responsibilities they will shoulder as they move up the ladder, from commanding a couple dozen service members as a junior officer to a few thousand as a colonel or a Navy captain.
Secretary Hegseth rightly understands that the PME institutions, especially at the intermediate and senior levels, play a critical role in shaping the strategic culture of U.S. military leadership. However, the Secretary’s guidance misdiagnoses what needs to change about that culture.
Since becoming a professional military, U.S. fighting forces have repeatedly demonstrated extraordinary operational competence. American military units are peerless as warfighters, and they have frequently achieved their immediate military objectives with remarkable efficiency, as was the case in both Iraq and Afghanistan. However, the United States has struggled to translate those battlefield accomplishments into meaningful political outcomes, which is the true measure of military effectiveness.
The ongoing conflict with Iran offers another illustration. American and Israeli forces easily penetrated Iran’s defenses, eliminated its senior leadership, and degraded the country’s missile and naval capabilities. However, nearly nine months after the conflict began, Iran’s governing regime remains in power, the Strait of Hormuz remains too dangerous for commercial shipping, and the Trump administration has failed to translate its immense military advantage into a durable political settlement aligned with U.S. interests.
Unfortunately, Secretary Hegseth’s guidance perpetuates this fundamental misunderstanding of what senior military leadership requires—and the shortcoming in American military performance that most urgently needs to be addressed. American military leaders aren’t lacking for training in how to conduct field maneuvers or win battles. No one underestimates the U.S. military’s lethality across all domains. But our adversaries almost certainly believe that America’s national security establishment fails to understand the fundamentally political nature of warfare, which dictates that tactical success is necessary but not sufficient to defend and advance U.S. interests in an increasingly contested global security environment.
In reiterating ad nauseum that “the fundamental purpose of the Armed Forces of the United States is to fight and win our Nation’s wars,” Secretary Hegseth displays a limited understanding of the role the military should play in deterring conflict in the first place, which requires more sophisticated thinking, and a wider range of coursework, than executing traditional battlefield maneuvers or even overseeing a theater-level military campaign.
Indeed, sustained deterrence represents the apex of military effectiveness. It requires understanding adversaries, anticipating their calculations, managing escalation, communicating resolve, and integrating military capabilities with diplomatic, economic, and informational instruments of national power. Preparing military leaders to advise civilian defense officials and contribute meaningfully to whole-of-government decision-making on the most consequential matters of state requires a much broader intellectual foundation than training them to carry out operational orders.
Consider Taiwan, a potential flashpoint for a confrontation between the United States and China. Deterring Beijing from imposing a blockade of the island, or even launching a full-scale invasion, is not simply a matter of developing the operational capabilities that would be required to respond in such a contingency. Effective deterrence requires understanding Beijing’s perceptions of American resolve, the political calculations of Chinese leadership, Taiwan’s domestic politics, the economic consequences of a conflict, and the credibility of American commitments to regional allies. U.S. military leaders who cannot think strategically across these dimensions, no matter how proficient they may be at operational planning and execution, will struggle to provide effective options to civilian defense leaders on averting what would almost certainly be a catastrophic military conflict.
These criticisms aside, there are several worthwhile ideas embedded in Secretary Hegseth’s direction, although many of its supposed innovations are already standard operation procedure at command and staff and senior service colleges. For example, emphasizing “jointness” among the services in PME is hardly a new idea. When I served on the teaching faculty at the National War College from 2019 to 2021, I did so as the Office of the Secretary of Defense Chair alongside several talented Warfighter Chairs seconded from the respective military services. And far from being “stagnant,” as Secretary Hegseth alleges, the PME environment surprised me with its agility. It continuously adapted its curricula, incorporating key lessons from recent case studies and experimenting with new approaches to preparing officers for an increasingly complex security environment—all while pivoting to a virtual learning en

35ac84bdb348.text: By — Samya Kullab, Associated Press Samya Kullab, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/zelenskyy-says-starshield-restrictions-threaten-ukraines-energy-defenses-ahead-of-winter Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Zelenskyy says Starshield restrictions threaten Ukraine's energy defenses ahead of winter World Nov 15, 2026 1:40 PM EST KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield satellite communications system are hindering its ability to intercept Russian drones, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday. He warned that limitations on the system, operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, could weaken defenses around Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of the winter months, when Moscow has repeatedly targeted the power grid. READ MORE: Zelenskyy says a new European security framework floated by U.S. could benefit Putin Ukraine's interceptor drones continue to lose contact with their operators when flying faster than 161 kph (100 mph) along the front line and over Russian-occupied territory, leaving them unable to catch Russian Shahed drones, Zelenskyy said. "We are counting on these restrictions to be lifted," he wrote on social media. "The protection of lives and Ukrainian energy infrastructure before winter depends on this. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Defense, and the President's Office have been instructed to work closely with the American side and SpaceX. It is important to be on the right side of history. We need to help Ukraine." Zelenskyy questioned Saturday whether the problem was technical, saying the restrictions appeared to have been imposed by SpaceX despite earlier assurances from U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Starshield was more under U.S. government control. Outages after Russian strike on power facility Meanwhile, a Russian strike on Chornomorsk, a port city in Ukraine's Odesa region, injured six people and damaged energy infrastructure, regional head Oleh Kiper said Sunday on Telegram. The blast and falling debris also damaged a gas pipeline and nearby residential buildings, while two parked cars caught fire. The strike hit a facility operated by DTEK Odesa Electric Networks, temporarily leaving about 41,000 customers without power, Kiper said. Overnight Russian airstrikes on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia injured another six people, including a 2-year-old boy, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said Sunday. Russia launched more than 2,300 drones, 1,590 guided aerial bombs and 15 missiles of various types against Ukraine over the past week, Zelenskyy said. Pope Leo rides in helicopter cockpit during Peru trip
Pope Leo XIV shared a cockpit with pilots from the Peruvian Air Force during his tour of Latin America.
Sharing the video to social media, the force said having the Pope join its pilots on Saturday was "an honour and an unforgettable memory".
On Sunday, the pontiff arrived in Cusco, a southern Andes Mountains city that was once the heart of the Inca empire.
There, the Pope visited an ancient Inca fortress, where he said religious traditions could help counter an age marked by "divisions, wounds, mistrust," stressing that faith should unite people and bring them together "in the light of faith and love."
The Peruvian leg of his tour holds special significance for the Pope.
He not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities.
